title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Patellar tendon rupture is a relatively uncommon but functionally disabling disruption of the knee extensor mechanism, typically occurring at the junction between the inferior patellar pole and tibial tubercle. The condition most often affects men aged 30 to 40 and arises when structurally compromised tendons are subjected to sudden high tensile loads. Predisposing factors include chronic tendinopathy, systemic conditions such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease, and exposure to corticosteroids or fluoroquinolones. The pathophysiology involves loss of continuity of the extensor apparatus, resulting in impaired knee extension and extensor lag. Clinical presentation includes acute pain, swelling, palpable gap, inability to extend the knee actively, and difficulty ambulating.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis relies on history and physical examination, supported by imaging studies, including ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging, to confirm tendon disruption and rule out intraarticular injury. Management typically involves acute primary repair or, in chronic cases, reconstructive techniques with possible augmentation. Complications may include rerupture, stiffness, or persistent weakness. Prognosis depends on the timeliness of repair, the quality of reconstruction, and adherence to postoperative rehabilitation.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to sharpen learners' skills in evaluating and managing patellar tendon rupture. Participants will deepen their understanding of the condition's etiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and best diagnostic and therapeutic practices. Greater competence will empower clinicians to collaborate successfully with interprofessional teams caring for affected individuals.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate complete rupture, partial tear, and intraarticular knee injury using focused history, risk-factor assessment, and functional examination of the extensor mechanism. Interpret imaging studies to confirm patellar tendon rupture and characterize tear features relevant to management, including patellar height, tear location, tissue quality, and extent. Apply evidence-informed, personalized strategies for managing patellar tendon rupture and preventing its possible sequelae. Implement postoperative rehabilitation and interprofessional care using protected early-motion principles, structured follow-up, and defined return-to-function milestones to optimize recovery and minimize complications. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction
content: Patellar tendon rupture is a relatively uncommon injury that disrupts the distal extensor mechanism, involving complete tendon discontinuity between the inferior patellar pole and the tibial tubercle. The condition predominantly affects men in the 3rd to 4th decade of life and typically arises when a biologically weakened tendon is subjected to high tensile loads. [1] Ruptures are classified as acute or chronic based on time from injury, a distinction that directly informs management and prognosis.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction
content: The knee extensor mechanism is essential for ambulation, providing active extension and resisting flexion. Therefore, prompt diagnosis and restoration are critical to prevent profound functional limitation. [2] [3] Surgical management is determined by timing and tissue or tear characteristics: acute complete ruptures generally undergo primary repair, historically via transosseous tunnels, with suture anchors increasingly utilized. Reconstruction using autograft or allograft options may be indicated for cases where primary repair is not feasible, particularly chronic tears or inadequate tissue quality.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Anatomy
content: The patellar tendon forms the distal component of the knee extensor mechanism, spanning from the inferior patellar pole to the tibial tubercle. Although its bone-to-bone attachment classifies it as a ligament, this fibrous band is termed a "tendon" as it is the terminal portion of the quadriceps tendon prior to tibial insertion.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Anatomy
content: The extensor mechanism includes the quadriceps muscle group, quadriceps tendon, medial and lateral patellar retinacula, patella, patellar tendon, and tibial tubercle. The quadriceps comprises 4 muscles: rectus femoris (originating from the anterior superior iliac spine and superior acetabular rim), vastus lateralis (greater trochanter and lateral linea aspera), vastus intermedius (proximal femoral shaft), and vastus medialis (intertrochanteric line and medial linea aspera), which converge into the quadriceps tendon and insert onto the patella. [4]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Anatomy
content: The medial and lateral retinacula constitute fascial expansions continuous with the vastus fascia and function as secondary stabilizers, preserving partial active extension and straight-leg raise (SLR) capability despite disruption of the patellar or quadriceps tendon. The patella, a sesamoid bone, increases the extensor lever arm and enhances quadriceps efficiency. Engagement with the trochlea begins at approximately 20° of flexion and completes by around 40°, while patellofemoral joint reaction forces reach approximately 3 times body weight during stair ascent and up to 7 times body weight during deep knee flexion. [5]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Anatomy
content: Structurally, the patellar tendon is broad proximally, reflecting the width of the inferior patella, and tapers distally as it inserts onto and invests the tibial tubercle. The mean tendon length and central width have been reported as 39 mm and 32 mm, respectively. [6] Tendon thickness ranges from 4.0 mm to 10.9 mm, with measurements exceeding 7.0 mm suggestive of tendinopathy. [7]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Anatomy
content: Proximally, the deep surface lies adjacent to the patellar articular cartilage and becomes continuous anteriorly with the patellar periosteum. Distally, the tendon narrows and anchors the extensor mechanism to the tibia. Vascular supply derives predominantly from the inferior-lateral genicular artery, an anastomotic network connecting the inferior medial genicular artery and the anterior tibial recurrent artery, with additional contributions from the retropatellar fat of Hoffa. Relative hypovascularity at the proximal and distal ends, compared with the better-perfused midsubstance, corresponds with the most frequent sites of rupture. [8]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Biomechanics
content: Regional variations in tendon loading and material behavior have been demonstrated. Biomechanical studies consistently show a flexion-dependent increase in tensile loading within the anterior patellar tendon, with relatively lower stresses posteriorly, resulting in higher peak and yield stresses in the anterior fibers compared with the posterior fibers. [9]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Biomechanics
content: Sagittal-plane analyses indicate that the tendon’s insertional regions experience strain approximately 3 to 4 times greater than the midsubstance, providing a plausible biomechanical explanation for the predominance of tears near osseous attachments. In structurally normal tendons, the load required to produce rupture has been estimated at approximately 17.5 times body weight, emphasizing that clinically observed failures typically reflect a combination of tensile overload and compromised tendon integrity.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Introduction -- Biomechanics
content: Mechanistically, rupture most often occurs during extensor mechanism overload with the knee in flexion against an eccentrically contracting quadriceps. In elite athletes, contributory kinematic patterns, including ankle plantarflexion and knee valgus, have also been described. [10]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Etiology
content: Chronic inflammatory pathology, including patellar tendinopathy, compromises tendon structural integrity and increases susceptibility to rupture. Systemic medical conditions that impair tendon quality further weaken the tendon and predispose it to rupture.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Etiology
content: Multiple systemic and local factors have been associated with an elevated risk of patellar tendon rupture. Systemic conditions that may compromise tendon integrity include systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes mellitus, and chronic renal disease, particularly in patients undergoing renal dialysis. Medication-related risks include chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy, prior corticosteroid injections, and exposure to fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Local factors, such as prior injury, repetitive overuse, patellar tendinopathy, and degenerative changes within the tendon, further diminish tendon strength and increase rupture risk. [11] [12] [13]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Epidemiology
content: Disruption of the knee extensor mechanism can occur at multiple locations within the extensor chain. The 3 most common sites of disruption are the patella, quadriceps tendon, and patellar tendon. [14] Patellar fractures occur more than twice as frequently as tendon ruptures. [15] Quadriceps tendon rupture is more common than patellar tendon rupture, particularly in adults older than 40. [16]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Epidemiology
content: Contemporary epidemiologic data estimate the incidence of quadriceps tendon rupture at approximately 1.37 cases per 100,000 person-years and the incidence of patellar tendon rupture at approximately 0.68 per 100,000 person-years in the general population. [17] Men are affected more frequently than women, a pattern attributed to greater muscular strength and consequent susceptibility to extensor mechanism injury. In contrast, women may be partially protected by greater ligamentous laxity and hormonal variations associated with the menstrual cycle.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Pathophysiology
content: Patellar tendon rupture results from tensile overload of the extensor mechanism, often superimposed on chronic tendon degeneration. [18] Rupture typically occurs during sudden quadriceps contraction with the knee in flexion, such as during stair ascent, landing from a jump, or abrupt directional changes while running. Tensile forces on the patellar tendon peak when the knee is flexed beyond 60°, explaining why most ruptures occur in this position. Ruptures can occur at 3 distinct locations. The most common site is proximal avulsion from the inferior patellar pole, with or without an osseous fragment. Strain at the tendon–patella interface is 3 to 4 times higher than in the midsubstance of the tendon. Other potential rupture sites include midsubstance tears and tibial tubercle avulsions.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- History and Physical -- History
content: Acute patellar tendon rupture typically presents with an abrupt onset of infrapatellar pain and swelling following a discrete inciting event, usually involving sudden quadriceps contraction during loaded eccentric knee flexion, such as landing from a jump or misstepping on stairs. Patients often report an audible or palpable “pop,” a sensation of giving way, immediate functional instability, and difficulty with weight-bearing.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- History and Physical -- History
content: History should systematically characterize symptom onset, pain location and severity, temporal progression, precipitating mechanism, aggravating and relieving factors, associated swelling or effusion, and the degree of functional limitation. Particular attention should be given to preinjury anterior knee pain suggestive of underlying tendinopathy, as well as systemic or medication-related factors that may compromise tendon integrity. [19]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- History and Physical -- History
content: Injuries presenting beyond approximately 6 weeks from the index event are commonly considered chronic. Partial tears may evolve more insidiously and are frequently observed in athletes who continue activity in the setting of patellar tendinopathy. [20]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Physical examination should begin with inspection for soft-tissue swelling, ecchymosis, and tense effusion, as acute patellar tendon rupture is frequently associated with large hemarthrosis. Comparative assessment of patellar height is critical, as patella alta relative to the contralateral side may be apparent (see Evaluation ). Palpation typically reveals focal infrapatellar tenderness and, in complete ruptures, a palpable gap or defect just distal to the inferior patellar pole.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: The hallmark functional finding is disruption of the extensor mechanism. Active knee extension is markedly reduced due to pain and mechanical failure, and patients are often unable to perform or maintain an SLR. Preservation of medial and lateral retinacular tissues may allow partial active extension or SLR, often with residual extensor lag that can obscure diagnosis.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Careful assessment is essential due to the prognostic impact of delayed recognition. Joint aspiration followed by local anesthetic injection may assist differentiation when examination is limited by pain or a large effusion, as true extensor mechanism disruption persists despite adequate analgesia.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Evaluation
content: Recommended radiographic evaluation includes anteroposterior and lateral views of the affected knee. In a complete rupture, radiographs may demonstrate patella alta (superiorly displaced patella). The Insall-Salvati ratio provides a rapid method to determine patella alta or baja (inferiorly displaced patella) on the lateral radiograph. This ratio is defined as the length of the patellar tendon divided by the length of the patella, ideally measured on a lateral view with the knee flexed to 30°. A normal ratio ranges from 0.8 to 1.2, with patella alta exceeding 1.2 and patella baja below 0.8. Radiographs may also reveal avulsion fractures or other concomitant knee injuries.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Evaluation
content: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most sensitive modality for diagnosing suspected patellar tendon rupture. MRI differentiates partial from complete rupture, identifies the precise rupture location, evaluates tendon degeneration, assesses patellar position, and detects concomitant intraarticular lesions. Ultrasound may serve as an adjunctive study, effectively detecting and localizing tendon disruption. Compared with MRI, ultrasound is less expensive and may be more accessible, depending on equipment and operator expertise.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Partial-Thickness Ruptures
content: Partial-thickness patellar tendon ruptures are generally managed initially with nonoperative measures. Acute incomplete tears with a preserved extensor mechanism are typically treated with immobilization in full extension and protected weight-bearing, often using a hinged knee brace.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Partial-Thickness Ruptures
content: Staged rehabilitation commonly begins with an early "acute" period (0–14 days) focused on mitigating the adverse effects of immobilization through isometric quadriceps activation and stretching, followed by a combined rehabilitation and return-to-activity phase lasting approximately 3 to 6 months. [21]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Partial-Thickness Ruptures
content: Emphasis shifts toward restoring full mobility and advancing concentric and eccentric strengthening during rehabilitation, with gradual introduction of jogging as tolerated. The subsequent return-to-activity phase incorporates dynamic, sport-specific tasks to enhance tendon elasticity and neuromuscular coordination. Adjunctive interventions, including dry needling, percutaneous ultrasonic débridement, and extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT), have been described. Outcomes vary, and the supporting evidence remains heterogeneous. [22] [23]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Partial-Thickness Ruptures
content: Available series indicate that a subset of partial-thickness tears ultimately requires operative treatment. Surgically treated patients consistently demonstrated greater than 50% tendon thickness involvement, with a threshold exceeding 55% reported as predictive of subsequent operative management. [24] Other series classified partial tears by ultrasonographic length (Grade I <10 mm, Grade II 10–20 mm, Grade III >20 mm), with operative conversion highest in Grade III injuries (38.5%) and lowest in Grade I lesions (6.6%), supporting the concept that tear length may help anticipate failure of conservative management.

content: Early clinical outcomes following surgical management of partial tears have generally been favorable in short-term follow-up cohorts. However, the literature remains limited, and additional studies are necessary to refine indications, optimal timing, and comparative effectiveness of different surgical techniques.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Complete Ruptures
content: Definitive management of complete patellar tendon rupture involves operative repair to reestablish extensor mechanism continuity, thereby restoring active knee extension and functional ambulation. Most complete ruptures occur at or near the tendon’s proximal attachment to the inferior patellar pole, although midsubstance disruptions are also observed. Midsubstance tears may present greater technical challenges due to inferior tissue quality and less reliable suture purchase. Surgical repair is generally indicated regardless of age or activity level and should be performed promptly once the diagnosis is confirmed to optimize biological healing and facilitate rehabilitation. A variety of fixation strategies have been described. Augmentation approaches vary according to tissue quality, tear pattern, and surgeon preference.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Complete Ruptures
content: Transosseous tunnel fixation represents the most widely used method of primary repair. [25] [26] This technique typically involves creating 2 to 4 tunnels through the patella, through which high-strength sutures are passed and securely tied to restore the tendon to its footprint. Construct integrity depends largely on the tendon–suture interface, making meticulous suture placement essential. Commonly employed configurations include Mason–Allen, Bunnell, and Krackow patterns. [27] [28] The Krackow technique is frequently utilized due to its locking running configuration and robust tendon purchase. Advanced imaging studies indicate that, despite multiple suture passes, this method does not substantially compromise tendon vascularity. [29]

content: Suture anchor fixation offers an alternative to transosseous patellar tunnels, with primary fixation achieved using anchors placed at the inferior patellar pole. [30] Advantages of this approach include limited surgical exposure, reduced risk of iatrogenic violation of patellar articular cartilage, shorter operative duration, and more anatomic restoration of the native tendon footprint. A modification employing cortical buttons in place of anchors has been described to enhance construct strength. [31]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Complete Ruptures
content: Repair augmentation is indicated in cases of compromised tendon quality, including fraying at tear margins or persistent gapping that threatens fixation stability. Augmentation may be achieved using high-strength suture constructs, cerclage cable wire, or biologic reinforcement with autograft or allograft tissue. The objective of augmentation is to reduce strain across the repair, limit gap formation, and potentially facilitate earlier progression of knee motion. [32]

content: Hamstring autograft augmentation is commonly employed, typically using a doubled graft incorporated into the repair by securing it within a distal patellar pole socket and suturing it to the native tendon. Transosseous repair reinforced with woven surgical mesh has also been reported to enhance resistance to cyclic gap formation following repair. [33]

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Treatment / Management -- Complete Ruptures
content: Internal bracing has emerged as an adjunctive strategy for acute patellar tendon repair, providing supplemental load-sharing support to the primary repair. This technique typically uses high-strength suture tape secured with knotless anchors to enhance construct stability and protect the repair during early rehabilitation. [34] A technical variation incorporates patellar bone tunnels combined with tibial cortical button fixation, with the suture tape whipstitched through the tendon to reinforce the repair construct. [35] Potential advantages of internal bracing include stronger fixation, earlier initiation of postoperative mobilization, and more rapid functional recovery.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of patellar tendon rupture includes quadriceps tendon rupture, patellar fracture, and tibial tubercle avulsion fracture. These conditions may present with loss of active knee extension and anterior knee pain, yet differ in anatomical location, imaging findings, and definitive management.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Staging
content: Grade 1: No demonstrable tear; tendon thickness less than 8 mm. Management is nonoperative and includes bracing, physiotherapy, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Grade 2: Partial-thickness tear involving less than 25% of tendon thickness. Treatment remains conservative with bracing, physiotherapy, and NSAIDs, with possible adjunctive use of PRP and ESWT. Grade 3: Tear involving 25% to 50% of tendon thickness. Management is nonoperative with bracing, physiotherapy, and NSAIDs, supplemented by adjuncts such as PRP and ESWT; dry needling may be considered where appropriate. Grade 4: High-grade partial tear involving over 50% of tendon thickness. Initial management is conservative with bracing, physiotherapy, NSAIDs, and adjunctive therapies (PRP, ESWT, dry needling); surgical intervention should be considered if symptoms persist despite approximately 6 months of structured nonoperative treatment.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Prognosis
content: Timely surgical repair of patellar tendon rupture is typically associated with favorable-to-excellent functional outcomes. Suboptimal recovery, complications, and repair failure are frequently related to diagnostic and therapeutic delays or errors in surgical technique.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Complications
content: Complications associated with patellar tendon rupture include rerupture, persistent extensor mechanism weakness, extensor lag with incomplete knee extension, knee stiffness, quadriceps atrophy, and infection. Mitigation requires meticulous surgical technique, appropriate fixation, structured rehabilitation emphasizing early controlled motion and quadriceps activation, and vigilant postoperative monitoring for wound complications.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: The postoperative rehabilitation protocol varies according to surgeon preference. The following serves as a general guideline.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: During weeks 0 through 2, the primary goal is the protection of the surgical tendon repair. Weight-bearing as tolerated is permitted with crutches and a knee brace locked in full extension. Range-of-motion (ROM) allowances are determined by the operating surgeon based on repair quality.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: During weeks 2 through 6, the goal is continued protection of the repair and normalization of gait with crutches and a knee brace. Weight-bearing as tolerated continues with crutches and the brace locked in full extension. Passive ROM from 0° to 90° of knee flexion is initiated, without active quadriceps extension. ROM progression remains at the discretion of the operating surgeon according to repair integrity.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Weeks 6 through 12 focus on normalization of gait on flat surfaces, progressive weaning from crutches, gradual knee brace adjustment to allow flexion, and initiation of active quadriceps contraction. Weight-bearing is advanced cautiously, avoiding flexion beyond 70°, while active ROM exercises are performed. Progressive strengthening includes physical therapy modalities, such as light squats, leg presses, and core exercises.

content: Weeks 12 through 16 aim to achieve a normalized gait on all surfaces without a brace, full ROM, single-leg stance with good control, and squats to 70° of knee flexion with proper technique. Nonimpact balance and proprioceptive drills are initiated, while quadriceps and core strengthening exercises continue.

content: Beyond 16 weeks, rehabilitation targets restoration of quadriceps control and pain-free performance during sport- or work-specific movements, including impact activities. title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Novel Rehabilitation Modalities
content: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) facilitates hypertrophy and strength gains using low loads. Tendon-related outcomes in healthy cohorts are variable but generally comparable to high-load or conventional low-load resistance training. Tendon-specific responses remain heterogeneous in rehabilitation settings. However, several studies report clinically meaningful improvements in pain, strength, performance, and condition-specific self-reported function. title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education should emphasize the nature of the surgical procedure and the critical importance of strict adherence to postoperative follow-up, particularly structured physical therapy. Nonoperative management similarly requires disciplined compliance with prescribed therapeutic exercises. Laxity in performing scheduled or home-based rehabilitation can result in permanent functional deficits. Realistic expectations must account for age, preinjury conditioning, and the demands of work and daily activities. Optimal outcomes are achievable with successful surgical intervention combined with consistent adherence to postoperative care and rehabilitation protocols.

title: Patellar Tendon Rupture -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Diagnosis and management of patellar tendon rupture are most effective when delivered through an interprofessional pathway involving orthopedic clinicians, physiotherapists, and orthopedic nursing staff. Management decisions should be guided by the extent of tendon disruption and the integrity of the extensor mechanism. Complete ruptures require operative repair because functional impairment from extensor mechanism failure is substantial. Early intervention for acute ruptures is strongly recommended to optimize healing, facilitate rehabilitation, and reduce the likelihood that delayed presentation will necessitate complex reconstruction.

Conservative management includes bracing, structured physiotherapy, and careful clinical reassessment to detect failure of nonoperative treatment. Orthopedic nurses provide critical support in both pathways by coordinating analgesia and medications, monitoring wounds and complications, reinforcing bracing and mobilization instructions, tracking functional progress, and promptly communicating clinical changes to the treating team.
